title: How Bail Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain how bail works, from its origins in thirteenth-century England (sureties) through habeas corpus, the Judiciary Act of 1789, and the Eighth Amendment, to modern cash bail, bail bondsmen and their premiums, collateral, property bonds, and release on citation or recognizance. They cover states that ban commercial bail bonding, and discuss Laura Sullivan's MPR series on bail abuses, including Broward County's pretrial program being shut down under bail bond industry lobbying and the Lubbock, Texas cases. They preview a bounty hunter episode two days later. The episode closes with listener mail about a Brazilian doctor who gave a blood transfusion to a child whose Jehovah's Witness parents objected.
topics: states that ban commercial bail bonding

segments.title: Opening banter and bail series introduction
segments.summary: Hosts joke about being arrested and booked, then introduce the two-part bail and bounty hunter series, prompted by listener Steve and an MPR series by Laura Sullivan.

segments.title: History of bail
segments.summary: Bail began in thirteenth-century England as sureties, persons who could be hanged in place of a defaulting defendant. Habeas corpus in the seventeenth century set terms for bail, and English Bill of Rights addressed excessive bail. The US adopted English common law and the Judiciary Act of 1789.

segments.title: Eighth Amendment and bail reforms
segments.summary: The Eighth Amendment guarantees bail and bars excessive bail. A 1966 change and later reforms closed loopholes for dangerous people, limited judges, and made bail harder for violent offenders. Capital crimes originally could not be bailed.

segments.title: Bail schedules and cash bail
segments.summary: Large jurisdictions such as Los Angeles use bail schedules that set fixed amounts per offense. Cash bail can be paid in full, by check, card, or cash.

segments.title: How bail bondsmen work
segments.summary: When people cannot pay full bail, they use a bail bondsman who posts a surety bond backed by an insurance company and charges a non-refundable premium, typically ten percent. Bondsmen take collateral such as property titles or jewelry and often involve family. Options like release on citation and release on recognizance are also described, along with property bonds where a lien is placed on property.

segments.title: Choosing a bail bondsman and states that ban bail bonds
segments.summary: Hosts advise checking a bondsman's license, fees, and responsiveness. Wisconsin, Oregon, Illinois, and Kentucky are described as having laws against commercial bail bonding, with Wisconsin doing so indirectly.

segments.title: Broward County pretrial programs and bail bond lobbying
segments.summary: The MPR report describes Broward County, Florida, where pretrial release programs with monitoring were successful and cheaper, but were shut down after bail bondsmen lobbied and donated to county officials. Lubbock, Texas, cases show poor defendants held for low bail amounts.

segments.title: Bondsmen not paying forfeited bail and bounty hunter preview
segments.summary: Bondsmen often negotiate forfeited bail down to about five percent. Hosts preview the bounty hunter episode and discuss Midnight Run and Dead Man.

segments.title: Listener mail: blood transfusion from a Jehovah's Witness family
segments.summary: A listener from Portugal shares a story about his father, a Brazilian doctor, who gave a child a blood transfusion against the Jehovah's Witness parents' wishes; the child recovered and the family later sent Christmas gifts.
